entries.title: Rename the lyx binary and the LYXHUB suffix (name clash with LyX)
entries.body:
Imported from [issue #670](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/670).

`lyx` collides with LyX, the LaTeX editor, which ships as the `lyx` package in Ubuntu/Debian and installs `/usr/bin/lyx`.
On a machine with both, whichever comes first on PATH wins: a shell where `~/go/bin` is not yet on PATH starts the LaTeX editor instead of LoomYard.
LyX is common among researchers, so the clash is likely for other users too.

## Name

The new name is open: `lyd` and `lyr` are the candidates, and the operator has not chosen.
Neither is an Ubuntu package name (checked 2026-10-17 and 2026-10-26).
Rejected: `ly`, since the binary and the `ly` plugin must not share a name (operator, 2026-10-26); `warp` and `ply` are Ubuntu packages, `weft` and `warp` are already fabric terms here, and the four-letter weaving names (`pirn`, `sley`) are longer to type.

## Priority (operator, 2026-10-26)

The rename lands before LoomYard is taken into use on other repositories, since renaming hubs and records already in use elsewhere is far more work.

## Scope

- The binary: the `cmd/lyx` build target and `binaryName()` in `tools/deploy`, docs and README, stencils and skills in the `ly` plugin that invoke `lyx`, and any scripts or launchers that call it.
- The hub directory suffix `-LYXHUB`, such as `loomyard-LYXHUB`, which the new name replaces (operator, 2026-10-26).

## Done mechanically (operator, 2026-10-26)

The rename is done by a script, never by hand edits file by file.
It needs agents to be allowed scripted edits, which `scripted-edits-allowed` brings.

## Runs alone (operator, 2026-10-22)

The rename runs alone, with no other run in flight, since it touches nearly every file; it is promoted and started only then.

entries.title: Parallel batches: the shared pieces for Webster forks and Weaver
entries.brief: DAG batchifier, worktree per batch, merge-back with conflict resolution; open: keeping a fork inside its worktree
entries.body:
## Seen (2026-10-17)

The pieces parallel batches need are the same whether a batch starts as a Webster fork or as a cold Weaver agent (see `weaver`); only the spawn differs.

1. A DAG batchifier: edges from the cards' targets and `Uses:`, cards joined into batches while the batch graph stays acyclic and under a cost budget, ready batches chosen. New.
2. A worktree per batch, created for the batch and removed after it. New; may build on fabric.
3. Merge-back of each batch worktree into the task branch, with a cheap model such as Haiku resolving textual conflicts. New.
4. The verify on the merged result and its failure ladder. Exists in Webster (verify gate).
5. The batch brackets and report: `begin-batch`, `record-batch`, the changed-files guard and the report contract. Exist in Webster.
6. `plan-dag-view`, to see the graph and the batches. Note filed.

## Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-17)

- Start with these pieces, built so both Webster and Weaver can use them; Webster can run parallel forks first.
- The hard part is getting a Webster fork to work in another worktree than its master's.
- Claude Code's own worktree isolation for agents has given the operator only trouble before.

## Open

How a fork is kept inside its batch's worktree: it inherits the master's working directory and a context full of paths into the task worktree, and `lyx` commands find their anchor from the working directory.

### Orch recommendation

Bench before build: a small proof of concept in which one fork is told to work in a worktree Go created, with absolute paths, and a PreToolUse hook refuses its Edit and Write calls outside that worktree, so a slip is refused instead of landing in the wrong tree; measure whether the fork stays inside and what `lyx` commands it needs a directory flag for.

entries.title: Recurring test-suite time and growth audit
entries.brief: Re-run cmd/testtiming against test-suite-timing.md to watch suite growth
entries.body:
## What this is

A recurring audit of test-suite growth, run with `go run ./cmd/testtiming` (Tier 1) and `go run ./cmd/testtiming -full` (Tier 2), and compared against the latest after-state in `docs/benchmarks/test-suite-timing.md`.
It replaces the per-package test-count budget that `test-budget-remove` deleted (operator decision 2026-10-17): count is kept down in review by `PATTERN-test-speed`, which absorbed `PATTERN-test-economy` in `04aafa88c`, and this audit watches the wall time and the per-package test counts that review cannot see in aggregate.
Each audit appends its numbers as a new section of `docs/benchmarks/test-suite-timing.md`, under the method that file states.

## What to look at

- Wall time per tier against the previous section, and the packages that moved most.
- Per-package test counts from `cmd/testtiming`'s `TESTS` column, and which packages grew since the previous audit.
- A growth with no matching new behavior is a candidate for a prune task under `PATTERN-test-speed`.

## Orch recommendation, not a decision

Run the audit every two weeks or after about 50 landed tasks, whichever comes first.
A cheap model (Sonnet) runs the measurement; the orch writes the section and files a prune task when a package grew without cause.

entries.title: Audit the twill and lens review setup: worth per perch, recurring finding classes, writer quality
entries.brief: One audit over the review records once about ten loom runs with the current setup land on Neve
entries.body:
## Questions

One audit over the same records (review files in the weft archive tags, `lyx report convergence`, `tools/tokencount/tokencount.sh`) answers three questions:

1. Is the lens fan and twill fixer setup worth its cost at each perch, and what should the standard review rounds be?
2. Which finding classes recur at Plan and Discussion, and where is each cheapest to stop at the source?
3. The open parts of the twill writer quality audit below, under "Data that would settle the open parts".

## When (operator, 2026-10-22)

Run it once about ten loom runs with the current setup have landed on Neve; runs from OSL-1046 are not gathered for it.

Later the same day (operator): run it now, over the loom runs landed since `504c5552` (2026-10-20), with the runs after `research-in-discussion` and `lenses-language-sets` (2026-10-22), which change Discussion, reported apart.

## Result of the first run (2026-10-22)

A sonnet agent ran the audit over the 6 loom runs landed since `504c5552`; the sample is small and only `finalize-dirty-names-paths` ran Discussion after the 2026-10-22 changes.

- Late rounds still pay: discussion round 3 found something real in 3 of 3 runs that reached it, plan round 2 in 3 of 3, nearly all new findings rather than too-narrow earlier fixes, so lowering caps is not supported.
- The lens fan raised 93% of round-1 gating findings at Discussion and 58% at Plan, for about $1 a perch; a review perch costs about $10-11, mostly in its later rounds.
- No further cut in round-1 findings from twill-plan is visible, and none is ruled out.
- Agent recommendation, not a decision: template defaults Discussion 2 soft / 3 hard, Plan 1 soft / 2 hard, Webster 1, Merge 1 (profile `light`'s values).
  Since `fed963ec5` these are no longer `light`'s values: the ladder is `speed`, `light` (1 round per perch), `solid` (Discussion 2, Plan 2) and `wide`.

## Operator decision (2026-10-22): lens fan in Discussion round 2

Since late rounds still find new things, Discussion-Review round 2 also runs the lens fan, and round 3 on runs solo: the hub's `loom.yaml` sets `discussion_reviewer_fan: ["review-discussion", "review-discussion", ""]`.
The twill fixer stays in every round, since many late-round defects are introduced by a sloppy fixer.
The next run of this audit checks what round 2's fan finds against a solo round 2, before Plan gets the same.

## Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-22): fewer, sharper lenses

Tokens could be saved by scoping each lens more precisely and having fewer of them.
A later run of this audit, with more material, measures per lens what it finds that no other lens or the plain reviewer finds, and how much of it is real, so lenses can be merged, sharpened or dropped.
The Plan writer's `twill-plan` fan comes first: the Plan lead carries a large context, and each of its lens forks inherits it, while the Discussion lead's context stays small.

## Review rounds after twill-plan (was note `review-rounds-after-twill-plan`)

The earlier audit below found discussion-review round 3 and plan-review round 2 useful only when an earlier round's fix was too narrow.
Since `504c5552` (2026-10-20), the Plan writer's `twill-plan` fan runs every `review-plan` lens, as the Discussion writer's fan already runs every `review-discussion` lens, which should cut round-1 findings further.
Compare those runs' round-1 Plan findings against the earlier audit's baseline, and check whether discussion-review round 3 and plan-review round 2 still find anything; if they rarely do, lower the default review bounce caps for those segments.

## Review setup

### Seen (2026-10-18)

- On 2026-10-16/17 every perch got the reworked review setup: a lens fan in round 1 (`review-discussion`, `review-plan`, `review-code` beside a plain reviewer), a twill fixer every round, and twill writers for Discussion and Plan.
- The setup costs tokens and time at every perch, and no measurement yet shows what it catches that the plain setup missed.

### Operator decision (2026-10-18)

- Audit the use of the twill and lens setup across every perch once it has run for a while, and set the standard review rounds from the result (see `run-profiles`).

### Orch recommendation, not a decision

- Run it after about ten loom runs with the setup, from `lyx report convergence` (stop classes, fresh-code fixes, review rounds per segment), `tools/tokencount/tokencount.sh` and the review files in the records repository.
- Per perch: how many findings each fan member and round raised, how many led to a change that stayed, how many the later perches or PR-Gate would have caught anyway, and the tokens and minutes each round cost.
- Compare with the runs from before 2026-10-16 where the records allow it.

## Plan writer finding classes (was note `plan-writer-finding-classes`)

### Seen (2026-10-15)

Over the 15 most recent full loom runs (`tools/tokencount/tokencount.sh -last 15`), Plan cost about $13 a run: the plan lead about $5.50, its forks (fork0 and the five lens forks) about $4, and Plan-Burler-Review about $3.80.
Each fix the lenses or the review ask for is work the writer did not get right the first time.

### Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-15)

Plan is heavy by nature, since it turns the Discussion into concrete work; the aim is a smarter Plan writer, so fewer Burler rounds are needed.

### Idea (orch recommendation)

- A fresh agent classifies every finding the Plan lenses and Plan-Burler-Review raised in recent runs: what kind of defect, whether it was real, and whether the review found something the lenses had not.
- Each recurring class goes where it is cheapest to stop at the source:
  - a machine check in `lyx loom validate-plan`, when the class can be checked deterministically;
  - a writer rule in the Plan stencil, when it is a judgement the writer can make up front;
  - a missing input, when the writer lacked something it needed (for example what `discussion-relevant-list` now hands it).
- Then measure whether lens and review findings per run drop.

### Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-16)

The lens fan and twill fixer (`fan-prompt-tuning`) are built first.
Later, this audit runs over real runs made with them, and the wording of the reviewer and fixer prompts is adjusted from what it observes, beside the Plan writer measures above.

### Operator decision (2026-10-16)

The Discussion and Plan perches run the twill fixer in every round; the lens fan reviewer runs in round 1 only, with solo review from round 2.
Reason: fixers introduce many defects, and a defect a late-round fixer introduces is seen only by the next review, or not at all at the hard cap.
The hub's `loom.yaml` carries it as `discussion_fan: ["review-discussion", ""]`, `plan_fan: ["review-plan", ""]`, `discussion_fix_fan: fix-discussion` and `plan_fix_fan: fix-plan`.
Orch recommendation, not a decision: the audit compares late-round fixer defects against runs from before this setup.

### Moved from note `perch-review-analysis` (issue #676, 2026-10-16)

The analysis measured rounds, tokens and late BLOCKING findings per perch; its classification of the late BLOCKING findings moved to `fan-prompt-tuning`, the lens fan and twill fixer it proposed are built there, and its proposal of two parallel round-1 reviewers is replaced by the lens fan.
Its Webster proposal (a hard cap of 2) is already met by the hub's `loom.yaml`: `webster_max_bounces: 1` with `webster_auto_accept: true`.
Two of its proposals are left for this audit to weigh, numbered as in the original:

3. **Later rounds review the fix delta.**
   A findings cannot be caught in round 1; they need a round after the fix.
   From round 2, one reviewer checks only what the fixer changed plus the sibling decisions or cards it touches, which is cheaper than a full review.
   Compare Traycer's incremental re-verify in #671.
6. **Measure again in a week**, with the same scripts: rounds per perch, BLOCKING share in round 1, and tokens per perch, before and after twill and the changes above.

## Twill writer quality, earlier result (was note `twill-writer-quality-audit`)

### Question (operator, 2026-10-18)

Has the quality of Discussion and Plan output gone up since the writers became twill-based?
An agent answered it on 2026-10-18 from the records (weft archive tags, Bolt config history, `lyx report convergence`); below is its finding.

### Short answer

Plan output got better when its writer became twill-based.
Discussion is the same or slightly better, which the data cannot show with confidence.
Adding the fork0 plan writer and the code list (generation 3) shows no further gain.

### Method

The main signal is round-1 BLOCKING plus MEDIUM findings of landed loom runs, read from the front matter of each run's `round-1-review.md` in the weft archive tags.
Each run is put in a generation by when its writer row started, checked against prod deploys and the hub config history on Bolt:

| Change | Live from | Set by |
|---|---|---|
| twill Discussion writer | 10-11 15:51 | `afd52a6f6` |
| twill Plan writer | 10-12 10:25 | `6099cd2bf` |
| fork0 plan writer (`2abb06c5e`) | 10-15 08:35 | deploy |
| code list (`530c339e9`) | 10-15 18:13 | deploy |
| review fan (`112cccb8f`) | 10-16 16:40 | `e57361ba5` |

Confounders and how they were handled:

- Baseline window 10-08 21:38 to 10-16 16:40, where every round-1 review ran solo on `opus[medium]` with no fan; earlier runs flipped reviewer between sonnet and opus (BLOCKING rate 0.69 against 1.32 per run) and are left out, as is `webster-replan-state`, which had a fan.
- After `112cccb8f` only five runs exist (`pr-gate-run-identity`, `creel-cli-output-fixes`, `shedrecipe-capabilities`, `creel-notices`, `orch-rules-files`); they are reported apart, not compared. The fan raises counts about 1.6x (5.4 to 8.8 findings per run at Discussion), matching 14 against 9.5 in `burler-fan-tuning-bench-2026-10-16`.
- `a273d69bc` only renamed keys; the models stayed the same (`25cc04048`).

### Signals

G1 is before twill, G2 twill, G3 fork0 plus code list.

Round-1 BLOCKING+MEDIUM per run (± standard error), and runs with any BLOCKING:

| Segment | G1 | G2 | G3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plan | 3.77±0.40, 26/40 runs | 1.72±0.30, 9/29 | 2.03±0.28, 12/33 |
| Discussion | 4.43±0.27, 20/28 | 3.57±0.27, 39/58 | 2.93±0.30, 6/15 |

- The first Plan runs (10-10 morning) are inflated by the switch to glyph-based plans (`78a2b1f14`); with Plan runs from 10-10 13:00 only, G1 is still 3.17.
- By task size in cards (diff size could not be resolved): the Plan drop holds in every bucket, 5.6 to 3.0 (over 12 cards), 2.9 to 1.7 (7 to 12), 2.2 to 0.4 (6 or fewer); G3 sits at or slightly above G2 (3.8, 2.5, 1.3). Discussion drops less: 5.3 to 4.8, 4.2 to 3.6, 3.8 to 2.3. G3 tasks are smaller (6.6 to 7.3 cards against about 10), and per card G3 Discussion is back at baseline (0.44 against 0.46).

Plan finding kinds per run, keyword counts over summaries, checked by reading about 15 runs:

| Plan finding kind, per run | G1 | G2 | G3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| design class | 1.43 | 0.62 | 0.48 |
| duplicate or over-specified tests | 0.38 | 0.03 | 0.15 |
| edits or tests no card targets | 0.35 | 0.14 | 0.12 |
| gate or glyph format | 0.75 | 0.31 | 0.12 |
| test branch no planned test reaches | 0.28 | 0.17 | 0.18 |

G1 runs such as `quick-recipe`, `config-layers-run-settings` and `driver-arbiter` are full of duplicate-test and missing-refusal-row findings, which the twill-plan lens forks target.
Discussion findings are the same kind in every generation, design holes such as unstated bounds and false premises (`lyx-halt`, `convergence-plan`, `fan-prompt-tuning`); design-class findings fall from 3.4 to 2.3 to 1.8 per run.
Wrong code references are rare in every generation and were not separated.

Rounds to converge, and circling settled by decision:

- Plan: 2.10 (5/40 circling), 1.69 (4/29), 1.61 (3/33).
- Discussion: 2.43 (10/28), 2.50 (21/58), 2.27 (2/15).
- Only `shuttle-send` (before 10-08) hit a hard cap.
- Rounds are confounded by Bouncer changes (`0ebdea27f` 10-08, `b2e4cf913` 10-11, `072e2ed86` 10-13, `85a8f3434` 10-14) and by sonnet reviewers in later rounds from 10-14 20:16 (Plan) and 10-15 07:30 (Discussion); within G2 circling halves after `072e2ed86` (14 to 7) with no writer change.

Plan gate failures: the Go gate retried Plan-Write once in the whole set (`tender`); the twill writers run `validate-plan` inside their session, so their failures are not in the records; no Plan-Write reran after 10-10 except `discussion-multi-llm`.

Downstream:

- Webster stops: G1 5/40 (`daemon-wakeups`, `test-suite-weight`, `driver-context`, `cli-surface`, `quick-recipe`), G2 2/29 (`tender`, `overview-seats` with plan_drifted), G3 0/33.
- Webster review rounds 1.98, 1.48, 1.12, but many Webster changes landed in the same window, so this is not credited to the writers.
- Webster deviations left out: their definition changed twice (`30385e1ae`, `493c62b71`).
- PR-Rework: G1 2/40 (`discussion-multi-llm`, `reed-hygiene`), G2 3/29 (`convergence-plan`, `reed-window-order`, `twill-fork0`), G3 1/33 (`creel-core`); no trend.
- Decisions added after Discussion: G1 11/28 runs (33 entries), G2 17/58 (37), G3 0/20; mostly parent design calls at circling escalations, which fell when `072e2ed86` and the alignment agent (`a40c7baef`) landed, so no writer signal.

### Verdicts

- Plan, G1 to G2: better, moderately high confidence. Round-1 BLOCKING+MEDIUM fell about 50% (about 3 standard errors even against the later G1 runs), in every size bucket, concentrated in the defect kinds the twill-plan lenses check; part of the format drop is glyph format settling.
- Plan, G2 to G3: same, low to moderate confidence. The bench predicted sharper fork0 lens catches (`twill-fork0-bench.md`); production shows no extra drop. The review rubric also changed in G3 (`9ea1f7474`, `e131c7625`, `27657341c`), and the code list (`530c339e9`) is mainly a cost change.
- Discussion: same or slightly better, low confidence. The 0.86-finding drop is about 2 standard errors, rounds did not move, the finding kinds did not change, and G3 is smaller tasks with the same findings per card; this matches `twill-discussion-bench.md` (contaminated, inconclusive) and `twill-discussion-fork0-bench.md` (keep twill, no fork0).

### Data that would settle the open parts

1. Blind real/noise grading of round-1 findings, as the bench grading did, on about 10 matched runs per generation.
2. A production replay: single writer against twill on 5 to 10 landed tasks from the solo-review window, with the same reviewer.
3. Plan-Write transcripts, to count `validate-plan` failures inside the session.
4. More runs under the fan review, for a post-`112cccb8f` baseline.
5. Diff sizes: for 113 of 179 runs the batch commits cannot be resolved in the prime, so only cards normalize size.

entries.title: Every remote operation runs async, and local-only fabric pairs stay an explicit choice only
entries.brief: Remote work goes async except the branch-exists check; batch pairs reach origin like any pair, and the local-only mode stays only as an explicit --local until a use is found or it is removed
entries.body:
## Seen

`batten-start-speed` builds local-only fabric pairs (`fabric add --local`, a local-only branch mark in `gitrepo` with a push refusal, pushes that skip such branches, and local modes of `fabric remove` and `fabric cleanup`): about 630 lines of code, 1360 with tests, plus a local-mark check in the status-push spawn entry.
The mode came from an orch recommendation in `weaver` that batch pairs never reach origin, which was wrong: a batch pair's commits are part of the implementation, and an agent continuing the work on another machine must see what a batch left half done.
The time it saves is small: in the sandbox hub `lyx fabric add` took about 1.1 s, nearly all of it two synchronous `git ls-remote` origin probes, with local work about 50 ms and its push already async; `lyx fabric remove --remote` took 6 to 7 s of network, at teardown, where nothing waits on it.

## Decisions (operator, 2026-10-18)

- The local-only pair mode stays for now, only as an explicit `fabric add --local` choice, since local work that needs no remote (experiments, local testing) may use it; no lyx flow creates local pairs, batch pairs included.
  Remove it (`--local`, the local-only branch mark and its push refusal, the skipped-local reporting in pushes, the local modes of remove and cleanup, and the local-mark check in the status push) if no use turns up.
- Every operation against a remote runs async, so no lyx command waits on the network.
  This includes `fabric remove`'s 6 to 7 s of network at teardown (force-with-lease push, archive-tag push, weft branch delete).
- One exception may stay synchronous: the check whether a pair's branches already exist on origin, since a branch found there is fetched and the work continued on, and that is worth waiting for.
  Today that is `fabric add`'s `git ls-remote` probes; they may run in parallel to cut the wait.

## Open

- Which remote operations are synchronous today besides `fabric remove`'s (force-with-lease push, archive-tag push, weft branch delete); an audit of the call sites belongs to the task that builds this.
- How an async remote failure reaches the operator or the orch.

entries.title: A small public NUnit repo as sandbox hub for end-to-end C# runs
entries.body:
## Seen

The C# path is tested only in unit tests over fixtures: no loom run has gone end to end on a C# repo, with a plan in C# glyphs, Webster writing C#, and the gate running `dotnet test`.
Models, the target repo, is proprietary and is never cloned outside OSL-1046 (operator, 2026-10-22).

## Idea

A small public NUnit repo of our own as a C# sandbox hub, beside `lyx-test-LYXHUB`, with NUnit tests, built with SDK 10 like Models.
Its projects target `net10.0`, not Models' `net9.0`: what the sandbox proves (build, `dotnet test`, filters, incremental builds) depends on the SDK, not the target runtime, and Neve then needs no 9.0 runtime (operator, 2026-10-22).
Runs on it prove the whole C# path on Neve before OSL-1046.

## Toolchain facts

- OSL-1046 has SDKs 8.0.32, 9.0.21 and 10.0.13 (operator, 2026-10-22).
- Neve has SDK 10.0.113 from apt (`dotnet-sdk-10.0`, installed 2026-10-22).

## Set up (2026-10-22)

The hub exists on Neve at `/home/knatte/Code/lyx-csharp-LYXHUB` (shortname `cs`), over the public repos `Knatte18/lyx-csharp` and `Knatte18/lyx-csharp-weft`: `LyxCsharp.sln` with three libraries and two NUnit test projects, `lens_set: csharp`, gate `tier0` running `dotnet test` without `Category=Slow` and `tier1` with it.
No run has gone through it yet; the first run there is the end-to-end proof this note asks for.
The first `tier1` gate run died with "Internal CLR error (0x80131506)" after 900 s and passed on a rerun; cause unknown.

## Regression harness (operator, 2026-10-25)

The sandbox gets a small capture/compare regression harness on the pattern of Models' `NORCE.Models.NumericalBaseline`: a capture writes scrubbed output into a gitignored baseline directory, and a compare mode fails on the first deviation.
It lets the Drift rows, landed in 1c344094a and off by default behind the hub-wide `drift.enabled` config flag, be proved on Neve, so Models on OSL-1046 is only the final confirmation.

entries.title: Move rules about lyx behaviour out of this repo's CLAUDE.md into lyx code, doc.go and stencils
entries.body:
## Seen

This repo's `CLAUDE.md` holds rules about how lyx itself behaves, which hold for every repo developed with lyx, not only this one.
Examples: in "Docs land in the same commit", that the task that builds a design never changes its own board entry's body or scope, that the landing marks the entry done and the board prune removes it, and that no decision, card or step of a run changes the running task's own entry; in "Production", how Batten's Land row runs the hub's `deploy` command and how `alignment_pr_approve` withdraws the alignment agent's landing.

## Idea

Two kinds of rule must be kept apart (operator, 2026-10-22):

1. Rules for every use of lyx, in any repo: they apply locally, to the repo the hub develops.
   They ship with lyx: what lyx enforces lives in the code and its package `doc.go`, and what agents must be told lives in the stencils lyx ships, so every hub gets them.
2. Rules for developing LoomYard itself, here in this repo: they live in this repo's `CLAUDE.md`, such as the cgo build, `update-plugins.sh` and the push rule for `main`.

Mixing them breaks other hubs: when the quarry hub was set up as a LYXHUB repo, its orch began taking in the LoomYard repo's issues instead of quarry's own, because a rule written for LoomYard development was read as a lyx rule.
`CLAUDE.md` is for one repo only, so go through it and move every rule of kind 1 out into lyx; go through the stencils too for rules of kind 2 that name LoomYard where they should name the hub's own repo.

The run-lock rule in `CLAUDE.md` (no decision, card or step of a run changes the running task's own entry) is a rule of kind 1: its home is the board's run lock and its package `doc.go`, so it moves out with the rest.

entries.title: Lens overlap audit: which lenses find the same defects, and a smaller set
entries.brief: twill-plan 8 to 5 lenses recommended; twill-discussion 7 to 4 and review-code 4 to 3 at low confidence
entries.body:
## Question (operator, 2026-10-22)

Which lenses find the same defects, which defect areas the lenses essentially cover, and whether a smaller lens set covers the same ground.

## Result (sonnet agent, 2026-10-22)

Sources: `_lyx/plan/lens-review.md` in the weft archive tags (94 loom runs, only 6 of them, all on 2026-10-22, with all 8 `twill-plan` lenses), the per-lens fork reports in the machine-local Claude Code transcripts (5 runs), and per-lens attribution in `round-1-review.md`.
The sample with the full lens set is small, lens texts changed over time, and a "fixed" finding only means the writer agreed; since `lens-fork-reports-kept` landed (79bab47a0) every lens fork's report is kept verbatim beside its record (`*.lens-<lens>.md` under `_lyx/plan/`, `_lyx/discussion/` and the review rounds), so later audits have per-lens data.

### `twill-plan` (8 lenses)

- `affected-set` and `forced-edits` are near-duplicates: 12 of `affected-set`'s 20 findings were also raised by `forced-edits`, 5 were its alone.
- `criteria-coverage`, `branch-coverage` and `row-reachability` overlap heavily; in one run all three reports led with the same three defects.
- `guard-reach` and `way-forward` overlap little with anything and each raised BLOCKING findings no other lens did.
- `test-economy` is 79% LOW and the most disputed, but its findings are unique.

Agent recommendation, not a decision: 5 lenses.

| Proposed lens | Replaces |
| --- | --- |
| `coverage` | `criteria-coverage`, `branch-coverage` |
| `row-validity` | `row-reachability`, `test-economy`, the nil-seam part of `affected-set` |
| `forced-edits` | `affected-set`, `forced-edits` |
| `guard-reach` | unchanged |
| `way-forward` | unchanged |

Merging `guard-reach` and `way-forward` as well is not supported by the data.

### `twill-discussion` (7 lenses), low confidence

Since 5e449651f `goal-scope` and `board-fit` are rewritten procedure lenses that also run in the `review-discussion` fan.

No lens-review file exists for the Discussion writer; one run's fork reports were read in full.
Agent recommendation, not a decision: 4 lenses, `decision-chain` (`interactions` + `walkthrough`, keeping the case-based procedure), `code-claims` (`bound-breaker` + `existing-paths`), `board-scope` (`goal-scope` + `board-fit`), `leanness`.
In the review fan, `bound-breaker` is the strongest lens (11 of 15 lens BLOCKING findings), `walkthrough` raised no BLOCKING.

### Review fans

- `review-plan` reruns the three lenses the Plan writer already ran, and still raised 35 findings in the six 2026-10-22 runs, mostly LOW and MEDIUM; whether these are bad fixes or new findings is not measured. Option: give `review-plan` the lenses the writer fan lacks.
- `review-code`: `code-affected-set` is the weakest (one MEDIUM in 18); agent recommendation, medium-low confidence: fold it into `code-pattern-fit`, which carries 7 of 8 lens BLOCKING findings, as one `code-consistency` lens, 4 to 3.
- `fix-*` fans: no per-lens data.

## Follow-up (operator, 2026-10-22)

- `twill-plan` goes to 5 lenses in task `twill-plan-five-lenses`.
- A later audit looks at the Discussion writer's `twill-discussion` alone, once enough runs made after 79bab47a0 have kept per-lens reports, and may trim it too.
  It matters less than Plan: the Discussion lead's context is far smaller when it forks, so its lens forks cost far less.

entries.title: Plan writer cost: sub-planners per part, and twill versus a solo writer
entries.brief: The Plan writer is 18% of spend; sub-planners per part for large bundles, and a twill versus solo Opus high comparison on cost, rounds and time
entries.body:
## Seen

`docs/research/token-audit-2026-10-22`: the Plan writer is the costliest session type, about $8 per run, $1,306 with its forks over two weeks (18% of all spend).
It averages 81 turns at a mean context of 223k, holds 153k by its first fork and peaks around 308k, mostly from about 71 raw `sed -n`/`grep` code reads.
Every `twill-plan` lens fork inherits that context, about 287k per turn; since 2026-10-20 the writer and its forks cost about $18 per run.

## Idea (orch, not decided)

Fork the lenses earlier, before the code reads pile up, or hand the writer a digest of the code it needs instead of raw reads.
Cutting a quarter of the writer's and its forks' cost saves about 4.5% of all spend; quality must be benched first.

## Discussion with the operator (2026-10-22)

- A code digest instead of raw reads is rejected: it is too inexact unless the code itself is read, and the writer would read the source anyway to be sure.
  Finding what to read is already `relevant.md`'s job; whether the writer uses it is worth measuring (how much of what the writer read the list named).
- Lens forks as fresh agents are rejected: that is the perch itself.
- Sub-planners: Discussion splits the scope into parts in the decision record, groups `relevant.md` per part, and each sub-planner reads only its part; the lead owns the shared spots and joins the card DAG.
  This keeps every review round and matters more as loom tasks are bundled larger.
  Review could split per part the same way, since each fresh reviewer rebuilds its context every round (Plan reviewer: 48 turns at 123k mean context, $2.48 per session).
- Twill-plan versus a solo writer: since the full `twill-plan` fan (2026-10-20), 7 landed loom runs average 2.00 Plan rounds against 2.09 before, while the writer's forks cost about $7 per run and a Plan round about $3.70; too few runs to judge.
  The operator sees strong signs that the twill writer makes a far better one-shot plan in shorter time, and time counts as well as tokens.
  Still, test a solo Opus high writer: compare twill, solo Opus high and solo Fable on Plan cost, Plan rounds and Plan wall time (`lyx report timing`) per run.

## Split writing: two variants to bench (operator, 2026-10-22)

Discussion-Write and Plan-Write already run as `shedadapters.MultiLLMProducer` over a `seatengine` table, a chair and advisors; advisors only advise, and twill is the chair forking itself, so today one session writes the whole product.
Two ways to have parts written separately, both benched against each other and against the twill and solo writers before anything reaches production:

1. **Seats with writing assistants.** The chair splits the scope, fixes the interfaces and shared spots, and hands each assistant seat its part; it then joins and checks the parts.
   A new seat role beside the advisor.
   Risks: assistants see neither each other's work nor a shared context, so seams fall to the chair and review, and overlapping parts make several seats read the same code.
2. **Fork-based.** The chair keeps its context lean (scope, split and shared spots only) and forks once per part, so every part writer inherits the same overview without the writer's full reading.
   Technically still one writer with forks, like twill but forking early.

## Data check (Sonnet agent, 2026-10-24)

Plan writer plus its lens forks, means per run (API list price):

| group | runs | writer+forks | forks | Plan-Write wall | Plan rounds |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| before 10-15 (solo writer) | 28 | $9.08 | $0.58 | 16.4 min active | 1.3 |
| 10-15 to 10-19 | 41 | $9.39 | $3.86 | 18.5 min | 1.88 |
| 10-20 to c62274be5 (full twill-plan fan) | 7 | $18.14 | $7.66 | 23.9 min | 2.00 |
| after c62274be5 (five lenses) | 3 | $16.64 | $7.40 | 23.9 min | 1.33 |

- The later groups are larger tasks, so the cost rise is not the fan alone; the five-lens group is too small to judge.
- `relevant.md` use, over 32 runs with a list and a Plan-Write transcript: 85% of named files were read, but only 28% of read files were named (about 3.5 files read per file named, about 7 on large runs). Both shares are lower bounds (directory greps and quarry reads not counted).
- So `relevant.md` works as a floor, not a boundary; most unnamed reading looks like tests and neighbouring callers, which a per-part split of the list would not remove.
- Still open: the solo Opus high and Fable writer bench, and the split-writing variants, which need new runs.
- Scripts, baseline tables and `results.md` are in `docs/research/plan-writer-audit-2026-10-24/`; rerun per its README.

## Discussion versus Plan: double reading (Sonnet agent, 2026-10-25)

55 loom runs seeded 2026-10-15 or later with both a `ly:<slug>:discussion` and a `ly:<slug>:plan` transcript on this machine; cost at API list price from the 10-24 tokencount reports, per run:

| | Discussion | Plan |
|---|---|---|
| phase total (writer, forks, review, fix) | $8.68 | $18.51 |
| writer session alone | $2.07 | $6.60 |
| writer turns / mean context | 39 / 89k tokens | 83 / 183k tokens |
| repo files read by the writer (pooled) | 1,093 | 3,286 |
| share read by both | 62% of Discussion's reads re-read by Plan | 21% of Plan's reads read by Discussion |
| same, without `PATTERN.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `pattern/`, `docs/` | 64% | 20% |

- Discussion costs 0.47 of Plan for the phase and 0.31 for the writer alone; Discussion was the dearer phase in only 4 of 55 runs.
- Plan-Write re-reads about 62% of the files Discussion-Write read (mean of per-run shares 62%), so exploration is repeated, but Plan reads about three times as many files and most of its reading (79%) is new.
- Rough size of the repeat: the Plan-Write reads that Discussion had already made are about 3.3M tokens pooled, about 59k per run (file bytes at current `main` divided by 4; whole files assumed, so an upper bound).
  That is roughly a third of the Plan writer's mean context, and it is paid again on every later turn through the cache.
- File-level only: directory greps, globs and `lyx quarry` reads are not counted, and a file is the same file by path, not by the lines read.
- The Discussion phase total holds its review rounds and fixers, which is most of its cost beyond the writer; the segment figures come from the 10-24 tokencount reports, so runs landed since are priced as of then.
- Rerun: `.scratch/discussion-overlap/reads2.sh <slug> plan|discussion` per run, then `analyze.sh`; both stay in `.scratch` and are not committed.
- Decision (operator, 2026-10-25): Discussion stays a separate step; folding it into the Plan writer would add turns to the costliest session.

## Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-22)

For the Webster perch Sonnet is the natural fit, since Webster's own forks are Sonnet.

## Idea (orch, not decided)

entries.title: Large tasks: Discussion, a pre-planner, and the pieces as darn runs inside the task's beam
entries.brief: Discussion decides scope, a pre-planner splits it into contracted pieces, each piece runs as darn from the task's beam, a whole-task perch reviews, then align and land
entries.body:
## Idea (operator, 2026-10-22)

A large task runs as a loom whose implementation is a set of darn runs inside its own beam:

1. Task A runs Discussion as today; Discussion stays the one agent that talks with the operator and decides scope.
2. A pre-planner breaks the decided scope into smaller pieces that together make up the whole scope.
   Each piece gets a contract: what it takes in, the behaviour it delivers, the names it exports to other pieces, and which pieces it depends on; not the inside, which the darn finds itself.
3. Each piece becomes a darn task with that contract and its part of the decision record and `relevant.md`, with `depends_on` between pieces.
4. The next producer turns Task A's worktree into a beam.
5. The darn tasks run from beam A as ordinary darn runs and merge back into Task A's branch, not `main`; pieces with no dependency between them run in parallel.
6. When every darn has merged back, a Task A-wide perch reviews the whole and makes small fixes.
7. The rest is as today: Parent-Align, PR, landing, so `main` takes Task A whole.

## Why

`docs/research/token-audit-2026-10-22`: a loom run carries a fixed cost of about $23, mostly Plan and the review rounds, and the Plan writer reads about 250k of context before it writes (91% of its peak).
Darn's fixed cost is about $2.60.
Split this way, each darn reads only its piece once, plans and implements it, and is reviewed by its own perch; Discussion and the whole-task perch keep loom's scope and overall check.
It came out of discussing sub-planners for the Plan writer (note `plan-writer-context`): pieces small enough to plan and implement together are darn runs.

## Depends on

The beam setup: `orch-any-worktree` is landed (dd11ab09f: beams, pairs from a parent pair, `lyx beam create`, `promote`, `land`), and `umbrella-daemon` is landed too (c2a03a885: dobby, a per-beam daemon that drives runs).
Earlier wording: `orch-any-worktree` (umbrella tasks spawning and landing from their own worktree) and `umbrella-daemon` (a daemon per beam that drives its runs).

## Open

- Contract precision: too loose and pieces collide, too tight and the pre-planner becomes today's Plan writer.
- A darn that finds its contract wrong stops and escalates to Task A instead of improvising; dependent pieces wait.
- What drives the darns inside the beam: dobby now starts and drives a beam's ready tasks (c2a03a885); open is how Task A's run waits for them.
- How large the whole-task perch's fixes may be before they mean a piece failed.
- Quality against full loom: each piece gets one perch instead of Plan and Webster review; measure follow-up fixes against loom runs.
- Cost: Discussion, pre-planner, N darns and the whole-task perch against a loom run of the same size.

## Review placement (operator, 2026-10-22)

- The pre-plan gets a perch, but the pre-plan is far smaller than today's plan format: pieces and their contracts, not cards.
- No perch per darn: a review per batch proved far too expensive in Millhouse, and a perch per piece is the same.
  The pieces run as darn with review off (`code_max_bounces: 0`, since `code-review-one-perch` made darn's perch the Code-Review perch), each still passing its own gate and tests; the whole-task perch after the last merge-back is the code review, as Webster's round over the whole diff is today.
  For scale, a darn perch costs about $1.30 per run in the audit window.
- The pieces run tests as they go, the way Webster's card gate runs after every card.

## Piece recipe `stitch` (operator, 2026-10-22)

The pieces run on their own recipe, `stitch`, derived from darn, not on a darn profile: rows go away, not only bounds.
Alignment per piece is pointless when the piece is a closed, synchronised share of an umbrella that is aligned whole.

- Kept: Preflight; the writer, on Sonnet, briefed by its pre-plan contract.
- Dropped: Code-Bouncer and the Code-Burler review/fix rows (review off), Describe and PR-Review.
  Since `loom-tail-review` (2026-10-24) darn has no Merge-In, Publish, PR-Align or PR-Gate rows; its Finalize merges the parent in under the lock.
- Finalize merges into the umbrella branch under the parent lock instead of landing on `main`.
- Friction-Reflect runs once per umbrella, not per piece.
- A `stitch` task runs only inside an umbrella; it cannot run alone.
- Estimate (orch, not measured): about $2-2.50 per piece against about $6 for a darn with review.

Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-24): once `stitch` exists, Codex could run the pre-planner, as a role apart from the Claude-written code (see note `codex-engine`).

## Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-23): darn itself as the piece implementer

Once `loom-tail-review` has landed, darn itself may serve as the pieces' implementer, since that task removes much of the run tail's ceremony, such as the pull request.
Whether `stitch` then stays a recipe of its own, or becomes darn with the tail rows a piece does not need turned off, is to be weighed against what `loom-tail-review` lands.

## Test depth of a piece (operator, 2026-10-23)

A piece run does not run the full suite a standalone darn runs before it lands.
The umbrella runs the full suite once, after every piece has merged back.
Which tiers a piece's own gates run is open; the gate key per recipe row is stated in `internal/gateslot`'s doc (`gate-runs-once`, landed): a piece's rows read `darn-write`, `code-burler-fix` and `finalize`.

## Pre-plan depth (orch, 2026-10-24, not decided)

- A coarse pre-plan leaves design to the pieces, so each piece needs an Opus writer.
- A detailed pre-plan carries the design, so Sonnet pieces may do, at the cost of a heavier pre-planner.
- Pieces cannot be counted on to run in parallel: `tools/plandag/plandag.sh` on `loom-tail-review`'s plan found 52 cards, a critical path of 20 and a mean parallelism of 2.6.
  A beam's gain is then mostly smaller review scopes, not wall time.

entries.title: Creel delivers agent mail in full at the receiver's next tool boundary
entries.brief: A reminder plus lyx creel read costs the receiver an extra turn per agent message
entries.body:
## Seen (2026-10-23)

Creel carries a message in full into the receiver's pane only when its sender is a program or EXTERNAL.
Mail from an agent strand, and any message over 4 KiB, reaches the receiver only as a reminder line naming `lyx creel read` (`internal/creelengine/doc.go`), so the receiver spends one extra turn reading it before it can act.
The reminder exists so that an agent's text cannot pose as an instruction in another agent's pane.

## Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-23)

With the runs' cost in focus, everything might instead be typed into the pane directly, with no reminder and read turn; to weigh later.

## Seen (2026-10-25, issue #871)

Creel delivers to a strand only when it is idle, so a receiver working one long turn gets nothing until the turn ends.
A parent decision for a darn run (`lyx loom decision add`, creel #280) stayed `posted` while the darn writer worked, though the writer works in one turn from start to finish.
Claude Code's SendMessage reached the same writer mid-turn, at its next tool boundary, without interrupting it.
`lyx creel interrupt` and `inject --interrupt` are no answer: they end the running turn and lose a tool call in flight, such as a long gate run.

## Operator decisions (2026-10-25)

- Creel delivers at the receiver's next tool boundary, as SendMessage does; interrupt stays for stopping an agent.
- Shape: creel stays the one router, with no separate post hub. It sets a flag file per strand while that strand has unread mail, and a `PostToolUse` hook tests the file and exits at once when it is absent, so a call with no mail costs a file test and no tokens; only when the flag stands does the hook hand over the mail.
- The hook hands over the mail itself, so the reminder and the `lyx creel read` turn go too.
- Codex: the spike (`docs/research/codex-spike-2026-10-24/report.md`) saw `SessionStart`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `Stop`, `PermissionRequest` and `PreToolUse` fire, but did not list `PostToolUse`; whether Codex can take mail at a tool boundary, through `PreToolUse` if need be, is checked in the test.
  The test task left the Codex part untested, since the Codex usage limit was reached (2026-10-25); its report gives the steps, and the check is still open.
- The hook delivery is tested on its own first, as task `creel-hook-delivery-test`, before creel becomes the one router and before note `creel-agents` is built.
- A strand that is idle fires no hook, so creel's delivery into an idle pane stays for that case; a turn with no tool call ends idle and is reached the same way. Each message is delivered once, by whichever path comes first.
- If feasible: a config key chooses whether Claude agents message each other through SendMessage or through creel.
  While only Claude runs, SendMessage is the better path; creel is needed where a non-Claude engine takes a role (note `creel-agents`).
  Programs, which cannot use SendMessage, go on posting through creel.

## Test result (2026-10-25)

`docs/research/creel-hook-delivery-2026-10-25/report.md` (eb3ccb3bd): for Claude, a `PostToolUse` hook delivered mail at the next tool boundary, each message claimed once across the hook and pane paths, at about 0.6 ms for a call with no mail.
The Codex part is untested, and the loss of the reminder guard stays open.

## To weigh

- The extra turn per agent message against the guard that keeps one agent's text from reading as an instruction in another agent's pane.
- Note `creel-agents` moves agent messaging from SendMessage onto creel, which makes agent mail, and so this cost, more common.

## Seen (2026-10-24)

A landing-stop halt at `Parent-Align` (renamed from `Merge-In` in 5e449651f) or `Finalize`, the merge fixer's `escalate` report included, goes straight to the orch: `internal/arbiterstop` marks it `LandingHalt` and skips the arbiter, and `landingshed.HandsBack` names it a hand-back.

## Idea (operator, 2026-10-24)

A fixer's `escalate` at a landing row goes to the arbiter first, as other stops do: the arbiter is a strong agent that can likely settle a decision collision against the decision record and what landed, and only its hand-on reaches the orch.
A spent cap, a failed or unusable fixer turn and an over-cap change stay as they are.

entries.title: Beams: one lyx beam start, machine ownership by project, and a beam's life as a pawl run
entries.brief: lyx beam start brings a beam up and resumes its orch; the overview window becomes beam: <slug>; projects, the root included, carry the owner machine and lyx adopt moves a project
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-25)

`lyx orch start` does four jobs: it starts every dobby this machine owns, reconciles the hub's branches against origin, ensures the overview window, and only then starts the orch session and its watcher.
Dobby's own verbs sit under `lyx beam` (`lyx beam start`, `lyx beam status`), and `lyx prime` names the top beam although the verb runs in any beam.
`--handoff` and `--adopt` are never used; `--continue` is used often and is long to type.
Ownership is recorded per task and for the prime (`lyx adopt <slug>`, `lyx adopt --prime`), although the prime is a worktree, local to one machine like every beam.

## Design (operator, 2026-10-25)

A beam, the prime included, is one unit of two parts that always run together: its daemon, dobby, which starts, drives and lands the beam's runs, and its LLM, the orch, which handles stops and questions and is always there to talk to.
Dobby already sends its notices to the orch, and an idle orch spends nothing until a message wakes it.
Both run on the machine that owns the beam.

### Starting a beam

- `lyx beam start [slug]` brings a beam up, the current worktree's beam with no slug: it starts the dobby, reconciles the branches, ensures the beam's overview window, and starts the orch with its watcher.
  The orch resumes its recorded session when one exists, else starts fresh from the last handoff note, else from the start stencil.
  A recorded session that cannot be resumed falls back to a fresh start from the note, never to an error.
- It starts only that beam; `lyx beam start --all` starts every beam this machine owns, such as after a restart, so the prime behaves like any other beam.
- It refuses in a folder that is no beam, a task worktree naming the beam it belongs to and its path; Ownership below says when it refuses on another machine's project.
- It is idempotent: a live dobby or orch is left alone, and only a missing part is started, a new orch resuming its recorded session.
- A new shortcut `lyx s` runs `lyx beam start`, then `lyx reed attach`; it attaches at once, so the operator never sees its output on success: what runs shows in the overview window, and a refusal attaches nothing and leaves its error on the terminal.
- `lyx beam stop [slug]` stops both, and `lyx beam status` shows both.
- A fresh orch comes from `lyx orch refresh`.
- `lyx orch` keeps `stop`, `status`, `distill`, `refresh`, `withdraw` and `rules`.
- Removed: `lyx orch start` with `--continue`, `--handoff` and `--adopt`; `lyx orch cleanup`, since `lyx cleanup` already removes old handoffs; `lyx prime`; `lyx beam promote`, since a beam is made from its project, never from a running task.

### Ownership

A worktree, and so a beam, belongs to one machine; the branches are shared, and the board's entries are common to every machine.
The board itself has no owner: ownership sits on projects.

- The top level of the board is a project of its own, the root project, driven by the owner machine's prime.
- Each project is owned by one machine and driven by its beam there; two machines can work at once on projects they each own, each with only its own project checked out.
- A task has no owner of its own: it follows its project, whose owner's dobby starts and drives it.
- `lyx adopt <project>` moves a project to this machine with its tasks and runs in flight, and `lyx adopt root` replaces `lyx adopt --prime`; only projects are adopted, never a single task.
- There is no adopt of a beam.
- `lyx beam start` refuses on a beam whose project another machine owns, naming `lyx adopt`.
- `lyx adopt` of a project starts its beam, dobby and orch, on the adopting machine.
- An adopt moves that project alone: a beam project nested under it keeps its own owner, so adopting root moves root's own tasks and never the beam projects under it.
- Landing a beam into its parent is the parent beam's job: the parent's dobby runs the landing and cleans up after it, so a machine lands a project only while it owns the parent as well.
  Example: with G and H beam projects under root and everything on Neve, OSL-1046 adopts G and finishes it, then adopts root to land G; H stays on Neve throughout.

### A beam's life is a batten run

A beam is made, landed and torn down by an ordinary batten run over its project entry, the same batten as for loom and darn: Worktree-Create, Run-Shed, Land, Worktree-Teardown.
Only the recipe Run-Shed runs differs: the `pawl` recipe, today's `beam` recipe renamed, since `beam` names the worktree; a beam project's entry carries `recipe: pawl`.
A pawl is the catch that holds a loom's warp beam until the weaver releases it, as Beam-Await holds the beam until `lyx beam land`.

| Row | Does |
|---|---|
| Beam-Up | marks the worktree as a beam, then starts its dobby and orch |
| Beam-Await | waits while the beam's own dobby runs its members, until `lyx beam land` ends it |
| Parent-Align | merges the parent into the beam, as loom's row does |
| Code-Review perch | Code-Bouncer, Code-Burler-Review and Code-Burler-Fix, loom's perch, reviewing the beam's diff after the merge |
| Beam-Describe | writes the landing description, as today |
| Finalize | merges the beam into its parent from inside, as for loom and darn; the conflict session resolves a conflict and an overlapping merge goes on to the landing gate, with no reroute |
| Beam-Down | stops the beam's orch, its watcher and its dobby |

- `lyx beam create <slug>`, run from the parent worktree, marks the project entry a beam with its owner and starts its batten run at once; it no longer makes the worktree itself.
- `lyx beam land <slug>` ends Beam-Await; it refuses while the beam has open members or member worktrees, and on a machine that does not own the parent project, naming `lyx adopt` of the parent.
- The separate landing run of today's `lyx beam land` goes.
- A beam's landing is the heaviest of the three recipes, since a project is large: where loom and darn only resolve a moved parent in Finalize, pawl aligns with the parent and reviews the result before it lands.
- Batten's start guard lets a beam project start, where it now refuses every project entry but a beam ready to land.
- When a beam's last member lands, its dobby sends its orch a notice that the beam can land, naming `lyx beam land <slug>`; when another machine owns the parent project, the notice says so and names `lyx adopt` of the parent.

## Seen (operator, 2026-10-25)

Darn's recipe runs Drift-Baseline with `capture: wait`, so the baseline row both records the scope and blocks on the capture in its own process, while loom splits the same work into Drift-Baseline, which starts a detached capture, and Drift-Await, which holds the run until the capture passed or the parent deferred it.
The two recipes therefore drive the same capture two ways, and `internal/shedrecipe/entries_drift.go` and `internal/driftengine` carry a `wait` capture mode that only darn uses.

## Idea (operator, 2026-10-25)

- Darn runs Drift-Baseline, then Drift-Await at once, then Darn-Write, the same two rows loom runs, with Drift-Await carrying `entry_gate: drift.enabled` like the other Drift rows.
- Drift-Baseline always detaches its capture; the `capture` config key and its `wait` mode go from `shedrecipe` and `driftengine`.

entries.title: Loom and darn Finalize resolve a moved parent themselves instead of rerouting
entries.body:
## Seen (umbrella-anchor, 2026-10-25)

A loom Finalize found that the parent's changes since Parent-Align touched files the task changed (`docs/overview.md`, `internal/beamcli/cli.go`, `internal/beamcli/doc.go`), judged the merge large and rerouted to Parent-Align.
The reroute re-enters the whole Code-Review perch over the whole diff, which takes long enough for the parent to move again, so a run can loop through Parent-Align and the perch several times, each loop a full perch's cost.
Loom, darn and beam run the same Finalize (`landingshed.Finalize`), with its conflict session and its merge fixer; only two flags set per recipe in `internal/loomcli/landingdeps.go` differ:

| Recipe | Conflict | Parent changes overlap the task's files |
|---|---|---|
| loom | aborts and reroutes to Parent-Align (`ConflictReroutes`) | reroutes to Parent-Align and the whole perch |
| darn | the conflict session resolves it in Finalize | reroutes to Code-Bouncer, whose perch reviews the overlap note |
| beam | the conflict session resolves it in Finalize | lands through the gate (`LargeMergeLands`) |

## Idea (operator, 2026-10-25)

- Loom and darn handle a moved parent in Finalize itself: the conflict session resolves a conflict under the parent lock, and an overlapping merge goes on to the landing gate, whose merge fixer fixes what fails.
- A conflict or overlap in Finalize no longer reroutes, so neither recipe re-runs its Code-Review perch for it.
- Parent-Align, before Code-Review, stays the loom row that catches the bulk of the parent's drift; Finalize takes only what moved since.
- A beam's landing is the opposite case and gets the full treatment instead; that belongs to the beam lifecycle task's `pawl` recipe.

entries.title: Adopt machine check: a gate key of its own, and visible while it runs
entries.brief: Adopt runs its machine check silently in the background under the finalize gate key
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-26, OSL-1046)

`lyx adopt --prime` on OSL-1046 started the machine check in the background (`lyx gate test --gate finalize --wait`) and printed only its pid and a log path, `_board/.lyx/adopt/suite.log`, inside the JSON.
Nothing on screen showed that a test run had started, how far it had come or how it ended.
The check exists to find what a move between machines breaks, here from Neve on Ubuntu 26 to OSL-1046 on Ubuntu 24.
The operator dislikes the gate key `finalize` for it: the run is the adopting machine's check, not a Finalize.

## Idea

- The adopt check runs under a gate key of its own, such as `adopt`, by the rule one gate key per producer, named after it.
- Its progress and result are visible from where the operator works: a window or strand of its own, or a line per tier to the orch and in `lyx beam status`, and a notice when it ends, failed or green.

entries.title: No test is skipped by design
entries.brief: Windows-only tests count as skips on Linux, and TestBuildLoomShed_OutputShape skips on every machine
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-26, OSL-1046)

The adopt check's gate run on Linux reported skipped tests in tier0 and tier1.
`TestUp_BootValidation/TmuxConfUnvalidatedOnWindows` (`internal/reedengine/lifecycle_test.go`) skips itself on every machine but Windows, so a Linux run counts it as a skip; tier1 has more Windows-only tests of the same kind.
`TestBuildLoomShed_OutputShape` (`internal/loomcli/sharedbootstrap_test.go`) skips itself whenever `buildLoomShed` fails, which it does because the test sets up no real fabric, so it most likely tests nothing on any machine.
Tier1 also skips the deliberate `TestCrossProduct` matrix cells (`internal/fabricengine/livestate_matrix_test.go`) and the child-process helper tests, which skip unless a parent test spawns them.

## Decided (operator, 2026-10-26)

No test is skipped by design: a test that is meant to skip has no place in the suite.

- A test that only means something on one OS moves into a file behind a `//go:build` tag for that OS, so other machines never compile it.
- `TestBuildLoomShed_OutputShape` either builds the real fabric it needs and fails when `buildLoomShed` fails, or is deleted.
- The matrix cells that are skipped by design are not generated at all.
- The child-process helpers stop being test functions the runner sees, for example by dispatching from `TestMain` on an environment variable.
- A skip that remains is a missing prerequisite, such as `TestGateTest_DotnetFixture` without its NuGet packages, so a skip in the gate log is always worth reading.
- `TestClaude/neither_skips/inner` in `internal/testkit/llmkit` is the skip helper's own test and stays.

entries.title: A read creates directories: state.ReadJSON mkdirs, so a hub reader leaves a real _lyx in a half-built pair
entries.body:
## Seen (scripted-edits-allowed, 2026-10-26)

Worktree-Create stopped with "warp repo already contains a real _lyx … it predates weft" on a brand-new task worktree.
The shed's tackler sent it back to Worktree-Create without finding the cause, and the second attempt passed by luck, about 40 seconds later.

## Cause

A hub-wide reader wrote into the half-built pair.
The `lyx batten overview` window refreshes through `orchcli.HubOrchs` (`internal/battencli/overview.go`), which walks every git worktree, a pair still being created included, and calls `fabricengine.ReadOrigin` (`internal/orchcli/live.go`).
`ReadOrigin` reads `<warp>/_lyx/fabric/origin.json` through `state.ReadJSON`, which runs `os.MkdirAll` on the file's directory (`internal/state/state.go`), so the read creates a real `<warp>/_lyx/fabric`.
In `Topology.Add` the weft worktree exists about 150 ms before `WireJunctionsWith` runs, and a poll in that gap leaves a real `_lyx` the junction check refuses.
The tender's `hubOrchs` (`internal/tendercli/deps.go`) takes the same path, and a read during staging also leaves a stray `.weft` directory under `.fabric-wt-staging-*`.
It can recur on any `lyx fabric add` while an overview window or the tender runs.

## Idea

- A read never creates a directory, anywhere: `state.ReadJSON` drops its `os.MkdirAll`, so only writes create directories, and a missing directory reads as a missing file (operator, 2026-10-26).
  Every caller that leaned on the read's mkdir, such as one whose lock file sits in the same directory, is found and fixed in the same change, and `ReadJSONNoMkdir` folds into `ReadJSON`.
- `ReadOrigin` and every other reader that seeds an exclude or a lock directory before reading stop doing so for a read.
- `HubOrchs` skips a worktree whose `_lyx` is not yet a link and every path under `.fabric-wt-staging-*`.
- `Topology.Add` wires the junctions right after the weft worktree is created, before writing the launchers.
- A test holds `Add` between weft creation and wiring, runs `HubOrchs`, and asserts no `<warp>/_lyx` appears.

entries.title: A mechanical plan conflict is fixed in Webster by a small fixer agent, not by a plan reroute
entries.body:
## Seen (beam-start-and-ownership, 2026-10-26)

`begin-batch 07` refused with `plan_conflict: tree_moved`, since card 16 still named two tests batch 06 had renamed.
Loom rerouted the whole run to Plan-Burler-Review: a new plan writer round and its perch, to fix two names in one card.

## Design

- A mechanical plan conflict such as `tree_moved` or `glyph-not-found` never reroutes to Plan-Burler-Review.
- A small dedicated fixer agent under the Webster run edits the named cards to match the tree, runs `lyx webster rebaseline --card NN` naming each card it edited, and Webster goes on.
- Only a conflict that changes what a card does goes back to the plan writer.

entries.title: Catch a renamed symbol a later card targets: in the plan writer, plan validation and a blocking batch-end check
entries.body:
## Seen (beam-start-and-ownership, 2026-10-26)

Card 6 (`recipe-named-pawl`) declared the function renames `NewBeam` -> `NewPawl` and `BeamRouting` -> `PawlRouting` as Rename pairs, but listed the tests `TestNewBeam` and `TestBeamRouting` under Edit only.
Batch 06's implementer renamed the tests too, and its report said "No departures".
Webster warned after batch 06 that card 16 had rename candidates, but only as information.
`begin-batch 07` then refused with `plan_conflict: tree_moved`, since card 16 still named the old tests.

## Design

- The plan writer handles it from the start: its stencil says a card that renames a symbol also declares the rename of the tests named after it.
- Plan validation flags a Rename pair whose symbol has same-named tests left under Edit.
- The batch-end check is blocking: when a batch removes or renames a symbol a later card targets, the batch gets a departure while its context is fresh, and the implementer either keeps the name or declares the rename.
